title: Choral Response with Feedback
preview: Ask short, quick questions the whole group answers out loud together. High energy, fast feedback, builds fluency.

body.summary: Choral Response means the whole group answers out loud at the same time, on your cue. You ask a short, direct question. You wait. Then you say "ready... go!" and everyone answers together. It's fast, it's energetic, and it checks understanding in real time — you can HEAR who hesitates, mumbles, or says the wrong thing. Used for 2-5 minutes, it's a great way to practice a skill repeatedly without anyone feeling put on the spot individually. Works well for vocabulary, procedures, quick facts, or checking understanding of a key concept.
body.whenToUse:
Use at the start of an intervention to warm up the brain ("what's 6 × 7?" "what does 'each' mean?"), or to practice a piece of a skill students keep missing ("when we see 'less than,' what do we do?"). Great when you want EVERY student to participate, not just the one who raises their hand fastest.

Avoid for open-ended questions ("how could you solve this?") — choral response is for questions with one clear answer.
body.howToImplement:
1. PICK 5-8 QUICK QUESTIONS. Each question should have ONE short answer. Examples:
   • "What's 6 × 7?"
   • "Does 'altogether' mean add or subtract?"
   • "What's the first step when solving 3x + 2 = 11?"
   • "Is 0.5 bigger or smaller than 0.3?"

2. EXPLAIN THE CUE.
   Say: "I'm going to ask a question. When I say 'ready... go!' — everyone answers at the same time, out loud. No raising hands. Ready to try?"

3. ASK THE FIRST QUESTION.
   Ask it clearly. Pause for 3 seconds (important — gives students thinking time). Then say: "Ready... go!"

4. LISTEN CAREFULLY.
   You're listening for: Did everyone answer? Was there hesitation? Did some students say the wrong answer or stay silent?

5. GIVE IMMEDIATE FEEDBACK.
   If they got it: "Yes! 42. One more."
   If they got it wrong: "I heard a mix. The answer is 42 — 6 groups of 7. Let's try this one."
   If you heard hesitation: "Some of you weren't sure. Let's try one more like it."

6. KEEP THE PACE FAST. 5-8 questions in 2-3 minutes. Keep energy up.
body.teacherMoves:
IF one or two students mumble or don't answer:
→ Don't call them out. Note it privately and make sure the next round includes an easier question they'll know.
→ After the round, say to that student: "Hey, I want to check one with just you — what's 6 + 4?" Keep it low-stakes.

IF students shout before your "go":
→ Say: "Whoa, I love your energy! But wait for my 'go' so we can all answer together." Restart the question.

IF most students get it wrong:
→ STOP. Don't keep going. Say: "I heard a lot of different answers. Let me show you how I'd solve this one." Go back to Think-Aloud Modeling for that skill.

IF the group is silent:
→ Lower the stakes. Say: "Okay, this one is a gimme — just answer on my 'go'. What's 2 + 2?" Build confidence back up.

IF you need a smaller version:
→ Pair answer: "On my 'go', tell your partner the answer." Reduces social risk of answering out loud.
body.variations:
TIER 2 (Standard):
Use as described. 5-8 questions, 2-3 minutes.

TIER 3 (Low-Stakes Start):
Begin with 3-4 questions you KNOW students can answer (to build confidence), then slip in 1-2 harder ones. Mixing wins and challenges keeps students willing to try.

THUMBS RESPONSE:
Instead of saying the answer, students show a thumbs up / thumbs down / thumbs sideways. Easier for students who are anxious about speaking.

MINI-WHITEBOARD RESPONSE:
Students write their answer on a personal whiteboard and hold it up at your cue. You see every answer at once. Great for problems where the answer is a number or a short expression.

ECHO RESPONSE:
You say the answer first. Students echo it back. Useful for teaching a new procedure or vocabulary term: "The word 'each' means ___." Students say: "Multiply."
body.researchBase: Choral Response is a core active-participation technique backed by decades of classroom research (Haydon et al., 2009). Engagement studies show that choral response produces higher on-task behavior and response rates than hand-raising (Sutherland, Alder, & Gunter, 2003). The What Works Clearinghouse notes that frequent, low-stakes practice with immediate feedback is one of the strongest evidence-based practices for building math fluency and confidence (Gersten et al., 2009).
body.inlineTip: Turn parts of this problem into quick choral-response questions. Ask the group to answer together on your 'ready... go!' cue.
